common_name: Wanda Primrose (Classic Deep Magenta-Purple Hybrid Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall or immediately after spring bloom; 'Wanda' spreads slowly into low mats and benefits from division every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun; 'Wanda' is one of the oldest and most enduring hybrid primroses in cultivation, a cross involving Primula juliae that produces low mats of bronze-tinged, crinkled foliage studded with rich magenta-purple flowers with a small yellow eye from late winter into early spring. Its extreme cold hardiness and tolerance of heavier soils than most primroses make it a reliable choice for cottage garden edges, woodland paths, and rock gardens alike. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season, and mulch lightly in winter in the coldest zones to protect the low crowns. Lift and divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain vigor and to propagate new plants for spreading along a border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early fall; like the species, 'Alba' goes semi-dormant in summer heat and prefers drier conditions once flowering finishes.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Alba' is the pure white-flowered selection of drumstick primrose, producing the same perfectly spherical flower heads on upright stalks as the species but in crisp white rather than purple or pink, which shows especially well against dark mulch or emerging spring foliage. It combines beautifully with the species' purple and rose-red forms for a mixed drift, and its pale color brightens shady woodland edges in early spring. Keep soil consistently moist during the spring growing season, and avoid letting the crown dry out completely even during summer semi-dormancy. Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering to maintain vigor and increase stock true to the white form, since seed-grown plants will not come reliably white.

common_name: Sunset Shades Cowslip (Warm-Colored Cowslip Primrose Strain)

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed in the refrigerator for 4-6 weeks before sowing indoors in late winter, or fall-sow outdoors where winters provide natural stratification; grow on in moist, humus-rich soil in part shade or dappled sun.

directions: Sow seed indoors after cold stratification, then transplant seedlings into moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to dappled sun; 'Sunset Shades' is a seed strain of cowslip that replaces the species' typical soft yellow with a warm palette of red, orange, apricot, pink, and cream nodding flowers, all carrying the same sweet fragrance as the wild form. It brings a cottage-garden warmth to woodland edges and shaded borders that the plain species lacks, and looks especially good massed with blue forget-me-nots or species tulips. Because it is an open-pollinated strain rather than a single clone, expect some variation in flower color among seedlings, and remove any that revert to plain yellow if uniform color is wanted. Established plants self-sow modestly and tolerate light foot traffic once dormant in summer.

planting.note: Plant dry tubers in late summer with the flat, rough side up about 1 inch below the soil surface in sharply drained soil under deciduous tree canopy that keeps them dry during summer dormancy.

directions: Plant tubers in late summer in sharply drained, gritty, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade; 'Bowles's Apollo' is a named selection of autumn cyclamen prized for foliage that emerges almost entirely silvery-pewter with only faint dark green veining, a striking departure from the typical green-and-silver mottled ivy-shaped leaves of the species. Pale to mid-pink swept-back flowers appear directly from bare soil in September before the leaves unfurl, followed by the luminous silver foliage that persists through winter and into spring. Because it is a selected clone, propagate by seed collected only from isolated plants to preserve the silver leaf character, or purchase named stock; open-pollinated seed near other cyclamen will not come true. Grow under deciduous trees where summer dryness is guaranteed and let colonies self-sow gradually into a silver-leaved autumn carpet.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like most named Erysimum cultivars, 'Bredon' does not come true from seed and is propagated by cuttings.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown specimens in average to lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Bredon' is a compact, mounding perennial wallflower bearing dense spikes of warm golden-yellow to amber flowers over gray-green evergreen foliage from early spring well into summer, with sporadic rebloom in mild fall weather. Its shorter, tidier habit compared to taller wallflower cultivars suits the front of a border or a large container without staking. Like other perennial wallflowers it is relatively short-lived, often declining after three to four years, so take softwood cuttings every year or two to maintain a supply of vigorous young plants. Avoid heavy or poorly drained soils, which shorten its lifespan and invite crown rot, and shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage a tidier second flush.

common_name: Constant Cheer Wallflower (Color-Changing Orange-to-Purple Perennial Wallflower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Constant Cheer' does not come true from seed and is propagated by cuttings.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown specimens in average to lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Constant Cheer' produces a striking succession of flower colors on the same spike, opening burnt orange and gold before aging through dusky rose to deep purple, so that each stem displays several colors simultaneously in a smoldering, ember-like effect quite different from single-toned wallflower cultivars. Bloom is nearly continuous from late winter through summer in mild climates, held above compact gray-green foliage. As with other perennial wallflowers, plants are short-lived, so root softwood cuttings every year or two to keep young, floriferous plants coming along, and avoid wet, heavy soils that shorten its life and invite rot.

common_name: Vindictive Sea Thrift (Compact Deep Rose-Red Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; avoid rich loam or clay, which cause the tight cushion habit to open up and flop.

directions: Divide and plant in dry, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; 'Vindictive' forms a dense evergreen tuft of grass-like foliage topped with compact clusters of deep rose-red flowers held on unusually short stems, giving a richer, more saturated color than the species and most other sea thrift cultivars. It flowers heavily in mid-spring and reliably continues with scattered rebloom through summer if deadheaded, making it one of the longer-blooming thrift selections for edging and rock gardens. Grow in poor to average, gritty soil, since fertile or moisture-retentive ground causes the tight cushion to loosen and become floppy. Once established it shrugs off drought, salt spray, and wind, needing only an occasional shearing of spent flower stalks to stay tidy.

common_name: Bevan's Variety Alpine Thrift (Deep Pink Cushion-Forming Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; a top-dressing of grit around the crown helps prevent rot in wet winters.

directions: Plant divisions in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; 'Bevan's Variety' is a deeper-flowered selection of juniper-leaf thrift, forming the same tight, needle-leaved cushion as the species but bearing a noticeably heavier crop of rich rose-pink to deep pink flower heads that all but hide the foliage at peak bloom in late spring. Its extremely compact size makes it a favorite for alpine troughs, scree beds, and tight pockets between paving stones, where its need for lean, mineral soil and razor-sharp drainage is easiest to satisfy. Wet or fertile soil quickly causes the crown to rot and the cushion to open up, so avoid amending planting sites with rich compost. Established cushions need little care beyond an annual grit top-dressing and rarely require division except to propagate new plants.
